lessons.title: Sector Rotation Patterns on the NSE During Recoveries

body.text: Sector leadership rotates through a recovery in a fairly recognisable sequence. Knowing that sequence turns which sectors are leading right now into a diagnostic for whether you're in early-cycle or late-cycle recovery, the distinction Lesson 4.1 built.

children.text: This lesson applies Lesson 4.1's early-versus-late-cycle framework to sector-level performance on the NSE. The sequence in which sectors typically take leadership through a recovery is not random, and once you know the typical order, you can use current market leadership as a cross-check on where the broader cycle actually stands.
The Rotation Sequence: A Working Framework

body.caption: Typical sector leadership through a recovery

cells: Beaten-down Financials (PSU banks, NBFCs), deep-value Smallcaps/Midcaps
Defensives (FMCG, Pharma), which barely fell and have little re-rating room left
Rate-sensitives (Auto, Real Estate), Financials continuing to lead, Metals/Commodities on operating leverage and global reflation
IT/Technology, still tied to the global cycle rather than the domestic recovery
Industrials and Capital Goods, as order books rebuild and capex resumes; broadening participation across sectors
Whichever sectors already ran hardest early and have less re-rating room left
Quality Largecaps, Defensives reasserting as risk appetite cools ahead of the next Peak
Smallcaps/Midcaps, already extended; high-beta cyclicals losing momentum

children.text: Banks and NBFCs tend to be the most beaten-down going into a slowdown, since markets price in rising credit costs and asset-quality stress well before it fully shows up in reported numbers, per Lesson 3.4's discussion of forward-looking market signals. They lead the bounce for three connected reasons: RBI rate cuts directly lower their cost of funds, improving net interest margins with a lag; credit growth stabilising, the Trough-phase pattern from Lesson 3.3, signals the worst of asset-quality stress is being priced out; and financials, given how tightly the sector tracks the credit cycle, function as a high-beta proxy for the entire domestic economy, making them the natural first mover when sentiment turns.
Why IT Often Lags the Domestic Recovery

Indian IT services revenue is overwhelmingly export-driven, tied to US and European corporate technology budgets rather than domestic Indian demand. This makes the sector's own cycle largely independent of the domestic recovery this course focuses on: IT can behave defensively during a purely domestic slowdown, such as demonetisation, precisely because it is not exposed to that specific shock, and can equally lag a purely domestic recovery rally, because that rally's catalyst, RBI easing, domestic credit recovery, domestic demand, is simply not IT's primary driver.

body.text: A genuinely domestic-driven recovery, the kind this course's framework mainly addresses, should show Financials, Auto, Real Estate, and eventually Industrials leading, with IT lagging. If IT is instead leading a rally, that is a useful diagnostic flag: the move may be driven more by global liquidity or a global tech cycle than by the specific domestic recovery signals this course has been building toward.

children.text: Smallcaps and Midcaps: The Amplified Read

The Nifty Smallcap 100 and Nifty Midcap 100 indices tend to fall hardest going into a downturn, higher beta, tighter credit access, and thinner institutional support all working against them, and then bounce hardest in the early-to-mid recovery, as the same factors reverse and cheap valuations attract renewed risk appetite. Late in the cycle, this typically reverses again as investors rotate back toward quality and largecaps, per the table above. Because of this amplified pattern, the relative performance of smallcaps and midcaps against the Nifty 50 is itself a useful, continuously updated gauge of what stage of the recovery the broader market believes it is in.

body.title: Illustrative Pattern: Smallcap vs Largecap Relative Performance Through a Recovery
Reading Sector Leadership
steps: Check which sectoral NSE indices, Nifty Bank, Nifty Auto, Nifty Realty, Nifty Metal, Nifty IT, Nifty FMCG, are leading and lagging over the trailing few months
Compare current leadership against the stage-by-stage table in this lesson to see which stage it best matches
Check whether IT is leading or lagging as a diagnostic for whether the move looks domestically or globally driven
Track Nifty Smallcap 100 and Nifty Midcap 100 performance relative to the Nifty 50, not in isolation, since the relative trend carries the cycle-stage signal
Cross-check sector leadership against the credit growth composition data from Lesson 3.3 and the RBI stance from Lesson 2.3 for a consistent overall picture

body.title: Diagnose the Leadership
body.scenario: Over the past two quarters, Nifty Bank and Nifty Realty have been the best-performing sectoral indices, up sharply from depressed levels. Nifty Smallcap 100 has also outperformed the Nifty 50 meaningfully. Nifty IT and Nifty FMCG have both lagged noticeably. Nifty Metal has also picked up, partly on stronger global commodity prices.
body.prompt: Which stage of the recovery does this leadership pattern most resemble, and is this move more likely domestically driven or globally driven? Explain using this lesson's framework.
body.modelAnswer: This pattern most closely matches early-cycle recovery, and it looks predominantly domestically driven. Financials and Real Estate leading, both rate-sensitive and credit-cycle-sensitive sectors, alongside Smallcap outperformance, are exactly the early-cycle leadership pattern from this lesson's table. IT and FMCG lagging is consistent with a domestic catalyst rather than a global one, since IT would be expected to participate more if this were primarily a global liquidity or global tech-cycle move, and FMCG's underperformance fits the early-cycle "defensives lag" pattern too. Metal's participation is a partial complication, since it can reflect global commodity prices as much as domestic reflation, so it is worth checking separately whether global commodity prices or domestic industrial demand is the bigger driver there before reading too much into it alone.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why can IT sector leadership during a rally be a useful diagnostic for whether the move is domestically or globally driven?
options: Because IT companies are legally required to disclose whether a rally is domestic or global
Because Indian IT revenue is overwhelmingly export-driven and tied to global technology spending, largely independent of the domestic credit and demand cycle this course's framework focuses on
Because IT stocks always move in the opposite direction of Financials
Because IT is the largest sector by weight in the Nifty 50
body.explanation: IT's revenue base sits mostly outside India, so its stock performance tracks global technology spending and the global cycle more than the domestic recovery signals this course has built out. IT leading a rally, rather than lagging as expected in a domestic recovery, is a signal worth investigating for a global rather than purely domestic driver.

body.text: This lesson presents a general, educational framework for sector rotation patterns. The chart is an illustration of a typical pattern, not actual historical index data, and past sector leadership does not guarantee future rotation will follow the same sequence. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation on any specific sector or stock.

points: Sector leadership typically rotates through a recovery: beaten-down Financials and Smallcaps lead first, Rate-sensitives and Metals follow, Industrials join mid-cycle, and Quality/Defensives reassert late-cycle
Financials tend to lead first because they are the most beaten-down going in, and benefit directly from RBI easing and credit growth stabilising
IT typically lags a domestic recovery since its revenue base is export-driven; IT leading instead is a useful flag that a rally may be more globally than domestically driven
Smallcap and Midcap performance relative to the Nifty 50, not in isolation, is a continuously updated gauge of which stage of the recovery the market believes it is in
